title: [Feature] Allow creating child loggers, or modifying the parent logger state
gold_answer: Staff said you can already pass your own logger with `.child()` when creating the Inngest client, but the types don't reflect that. They plan to extend the passed logger's type so `.child()` is available in functions. Exposing `logger` inside middleware, which would enable the other proposed approaches, was noted as a limiting factor, with no shipped fix yet.
gold_thread:
Hi, @mcky! 👋

Thanks loads for this detailed write-up.

I believe you _should_ be able to bring your own child-compatible logger if you pass a logger with a `.child()` when creating your client, but aye, types won't reflect that, meaning you don't have access to it. We could perhaps simply extend whatever logger you pass there, ensuring you have all of the usual methods (like `.child()`), then this would be less of a problem.

That feels like the best immediate fix, but you raise some good points about middleware and not having access to everything you need. After the fix above, I guess the limiting factor stopping you achieving any of your listed solutions (without patching) is not being able to access `logger` within the middleware hooks?

The logging itself is, internally, middleware, which currently doesn't appear when creating extra middleware. If you _did_ have access to `logger` within your middleware, you could shim it nicely and have the ability to add tools you're wanting such as `setMeta`.

title: [Feature] Add middleware callback with step info before each step is ran
gold_answer: Staff confirmed that `beforeExecution()` fires when the function starts executing new code, not before each step, so it can't report the upcoming step name. They proposed new step-level hooks, `beforeStepExecution()` (with step info) and `afterStepExecution()` (with the result), as a missing piece in middleware. The thread does not show these hooks shipping.
gold_thread:
Hi @mcky! 👋

Ah - this is a perfect use case and something we want to get right for middleware to make sure it's not restrictive. The debugging middleware in #217 is actually entirely middleware (no internals at all), but it's still lacking the accuracy you're wanting here.

The technical detail here is that `beforeExecution()` tracks when we're about to begin executing new code in the function as a whole - not necessarily a new step. In addition, it may be the case that we call the hook, execute the function as a whole, and _then_ decide to run a step in the same execution. Calling the same hook twice would be a bit confusing, I think.

It sounds to me like this might warrant a new hook that clearly marks when we're running a step, like `beforeStepExcecution()` and `afterStepExecution()`.

- Function hooks
  - `beforeExecution()` - starting to execute new code in the function
  - `afterExecution()` - finished executing the function
- Step hooks
  - <kbd>NEW</kbd> `beforeStepExecution()` - starting to execute a step (includes that step info)
  - <kbd>NEW</kbd> `afterStepExecution()` - finished executing the step (includes result, similar to `transformOutput()`)

We've seen this requirement pop up before - I think it may be a missing piece in our hooks right now.

re: p.s. - Yes! 🙌 Diagrams of when these hooks run would be great. I'm thinking a controllable animation that steps over code on one side and hooks on the other might be good. 🤔

title: ESM Module Error: @dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod compatibility with agent-kit
question:
## Bug Description
When using the latest version of @inngest/agent-kit (v0.3.0) with Next.js, I'm encountering an ESM/CommonJS compatibility issue. The agent-kit package tries to import @dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod using CommonJS require(), but that package is an ESM module.

When using @inngest/agent-kit v0.2.2:

 ⨯ [Error: require() of ES Module /Users/ruby/code/nexus-workflow/node_modules/@dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod/dist/index.js from /Users/ruby/code/nexus-workflow/node_modules/@inngest/agent-kit/dist/agent.js not supported.
Instead change the require of index.js in /Users/ruby/code/nexus-workflow/node_modules/@inngest/agent-kit/dist/agent.js to a dynamic import() which is available in all CommonJS modules.] {
  code: 'ERR_REQUIRE_ESM'
}



## Environment
- Next.js: 15.1.3
- @inngest/agent-kit: Tested v0.1.2 (works), v0.2.2 and v0.3.0 (both fail)
- inngest: 3.31.11
- React: 19.0.0
- Node.js version: 20.15.1

## Reproduction Steps
1. Set up a Next.js project with dependencies as listed above
2. Install @inngest/agent-kit v0.1.2 (works correctly)
3. Upgrade to @inngest/agent-kit v0.2.2 or v0.3.0
4. Run the development server (npm run dev)
5. The server fails with ESM/CommonJS compatibility errors

## Attempted Solutions
I've tried various workarounds including:
- Adding transpilePackages: ['@inngest/agent-kit', '@dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod'] to next.config.js
- Setting experimental.esmExternals to 'loose' in next.config.js
- Creating a bridge module that avoids using agent-kit directly and falls back to inngest.step.ai.infer()
- Modifying webpack configuration to handle ESM modules
- Downgrading from v0.3.0 to v0.2.2 (but encountered similar errors with pkce-challenge)

None of these solutions have fully resolved the issue. The only version that works correctly is v0.1.2, but it lacks the newer features I need.

## Suggested Fix
The agent-kit package should be updated to:
1. Use dynamic import() instead of require() when importing ESM modules
2. Provide a compatibility layer for both ESM and CommonJS environments
3. Update dependencies to versions that support dual module systems

This issue affects the usability of agent-kit in Next.js projects, which is a common use case for Inngest functions.
gold_answer: The ERR_REQUIRE_ESM error comes from agent-kit importing the ESM-only @dmitryrechkin/json-schema-to-zod with require(). Upgrading to @inngest/agent-kit@0.3.1, which ships both CJS and ESM builds, resolves it.
gold_thread:
Thanks for the detailed report, @eraykeskinmac!

Could you try using `@inngest/agent-kit@0.3.1`? This offers dual CJS and ESM builds so may resolve the issue immediately.

If not, we can ship another change to handle this case.
---
Awesome! Thanks for testing and glad it's looking good, @eraykeskinmac! 🙌 

cc @MonsterDeveloper - thanks for the PR 🙂

title: Self-Hosted dashboard authentication
question:
Hi everyone,

I have a question regarding the security of the dashboard UI when self-hosting:

- Does Inngest provide built-in authentication mechanisms for the dashboard, or should we implement our own authentication layer? and if yes, how?
- Are there any specific configurations or middleware you suggest to restrict access to authorized users only?

I want to ensure that the dashboard is secure and accessible only to authorized personnel within our organization.

Any guidance or documentation you could provide would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks in advance for your help.
gold_answer: Self-hosted Inngest does not include built-in dashboard auth. The recommended workaround is to put the dashboard behind a reverse proxy or load balancer with authentication (such as nginx basic auth), and to route the event/API endpoints on a separate domain so Inngest can still reach them. Staff noted auth support is not currently planned, but contributions to the inngest/inngest repo are welcome.
gold_thread:
Currently, self-hosted Inngest doesn't provide auth. The best path forward for now is @sathishkannan162's suggestion. 

If we did add support for auth, what type of setup would you like to see? We could potentially add Github or Google auth as an option, but it would take some time. We'd also be open to contributions in our [inngest](https://github.com/inngest/inngest) repo if you're interested.

title: Question about Pro plan concurrency limits (100 concurrent steps feels very low?)
question:
Hi team,

I’m evaluating Inngest for LLM-heavy workloads, and I’m struggling to understand the reasoning behind the Pro plan concurrency limit of 100 concurrent steps.

From my perspective, 100 concurrent executing steps (account-wide) feels extremely low for modern AI / LLM-driven systems. If each step represents something like an in-flight LLM call, this effectively caps parallelism at 100 across the entire environment.

For batch-style processing or even moderately high-traffic SaaS workloads, this seems like a very tight ceiling. It makes me wonder:
- What’s the design philosophy behind keeping concurrency this low?
- Is Inngest primarily optimized for orchestration rather than high-parallel compute?
- Are most production users expected to stay well under 100 concurrent active steps?
- In what kinds of real-world workloads does 100 concurrency not become a bottleneck?

From the outside, it feels like this limit removes much of the benefit of using Inngest for large-scale fan-out workflows (e.g., thousands of LLM tasks). I’d love to understand the architectural or economic reasoning behind this constraint.

Appreciate any insight into how the team thinks about concurrency and scaling at higher volumes.

Thanks!
gold_answer: The Pro plan includes 100 concurrent steps as a base amount, but concurrency is not capped at 100. Customers can add on more concurrency as needed, and teams at high scale can move to Enterprise/custom plans for the highest loads.
gold_thread:
Hi @softmarshmallow, 
The Pro plan _starts_ at 100 concurrent steps, but you can choose to add on as much more concurrency that you need. 100 is not a limit; it's the base included amount.

Many of our customers add on additional concurrency to handle the types of workloads that they need. Also, many customers run high throughput, highly parallelized workloads, but they often increase their concurrency and many teams at high scale will move to enterprise/custom plans for the highest load scenarios. 

The Pro plan aims to be a plan that works for many types of companies, enabling folks to increase certain areas via add-ons (ex. concurrency, advanced o11y/extended history, support) and scale usage (e.g. executions) over time with tiers that get cheaper as you scale. Some teams have important low throughput workloads and others have high throughput or bursty workloads and need more concurrency. As additional concurrent load requires additional capacity on our servers, we associate a cost with this.

As a question for you, was it clear from our pricing page that it's possible to add on more concurrent steps/capacity? Or not?

Thanks for your question!

title: support waiting on multiple events in step
gold_answer: Promise.race() works for waiting on multiple events in a step, and Inngest's suggested waitForAny() helper can optimize this by avoiding re-running the function as often. If timeouts are aligned, the two approaches are basically equivalent; with differing timeouts, waitForAny() won't resolve early and instead returns null when a shorter timeout fires.
gold_thread:
Hi @oieduardorabelo - I'll answer your question in #315 here!

You can totally use `Promise.race()` too! Using the `waitForAny()` I suggested in the other thread _does_ give Inngest the chance to optimize the execution of that function a little, as `Promise.race()` requires that we're revisiting your function as often as we can.

In addition, if in this case you had differing timeouts, the `waitForAny()` snippet wouldn't resolve early, though with if you had a race with a 10s and a 20s timeout and the 10s timed out, that'd resolve with `null`.

It's small differences really; if you're happy with aligning timeouts then it's basically the same!

title: How to implement webhook to inform user that background job has been completed?
question:
Hi, i have successfully implemented inngest in my web app to allow the job to handed off to be run in the background

However, how can I notify my user in my frontend when the background job has been completed?

Anyone has done a successful implementation of the inngest webhook to share the code snippet or can be point to some good resource for me to do my research on how to implement webhook to inform user that background job has been completed. Thanks a lot
gold_answer: Staff suggested three options: use Inngest Realtime to push updates from the function to the browser, poll the run status through the REST API via a backend endpoint in your app, or add a final step.run that writes to your database or notification system to notify users.
gold_thread:
Hi @myhendry, Inngest has a couple options that you can use:

* **Realtime** - Push updates to the browser from your function: https://www.inngest.com/docs/features/realtime
* **REST API** - You can fetch the status of a run via the REST API. [Here's some guidance on make this request](https://www.inngest.com/docs/examples/fetch-run-status-and-output). This request would have to happen via your backend/API, so you could wrap this in an API endpoint in your application.

Alternatively, you could add an extra `step.run` to interact with a database or notification system that you may already have set up to push an update to your users.

title: How could I add an instance of logger to the async context?
gold_answer: Get the logger from the function's context in the middleware's transformInput() hook (ctx.logger) inside onFunctionRun, because the built-in logger is internally middleware and its types aren't exposed to userland middleware. Store it in AsyncLocalStorage in beforeExecution and remove it in afterExecution.

title: Can you nest steps in a function?
gold_answer: Inngest doesn't support nesting steps (calling step.run inside step.run). Group related steps with a regular async function that calls step.run sequentially, or run the sub-steps as a separate function via step.invoke.
